newsitem.title: UK: UK to end grievance of disaster village Aberfan.
newsitem.headline: UK to end grievance of disaster village Aberfan.

text.p: Thirty-one years after the Welsh village of Aberfan lost dozens of its children in a coal tip disaster, the government is to address a long-standing grievance over the handling of the tragedy.

Welsh Secretary Ron Davies announced that 150,000 pounds ($245,200) taken from a Disaster Fund to help level coal tips round the village following the collapse of one of them onto the village school, will be repaid.
The landslide in 1966 followed four days of October rain and killed 116 children and 28 adults.

The use of the Disaster Fund money has long rankled with villagers. They argued that the fund, which received contributions from thousands of Britons, should be used to help grieving families and set up memorials to the dead.

The Labour government of the day at first suggested that "local interests" should bear a third of the 1.25 million pound cost of getting rid of the spoil tips, but eventually agreed to accept a smaller sum.
But Davies said even this had been wrong. "The Disaster Fund should never have been required to contribute to the removal of the tips," he said in a written answer to a parliamentary question.
Aberfan, once one of dozens of mining villages in South Wales, no longer has a local pit.
Davies said he will be contacting the Disaster Fund to consult on how the returned money should be spent. ($1=.6118 Pound)
